A bare wooden mallet head gives a sharper attack, one covered with leather, cloth or tape a softer one; hard mallets are usual in the West, soft ones in Asia. The size of the body varies with the number of strings over the bridges, and the 15/14 model reaches three octaves. Unlike a plucked zither it is sounded by striking; like the piano it is a struck chordophone, but the player holds the mallets and strikes directly.

The type common in medieval Western Europe derives from the plucked psaltery and appears in documents and images from the early fifteenth century. In the mid-1930s Tobi Reizer and others in the Alpine region developed the Salzburg chromatic hackbrett, which entered state-funded music schools after the war; in the English-speaking world the four-note grouping marks on most hammered dulcimers were introduced by Sam Rizzetta in the 1960s.

哈克佈雷特敲擊琴屬齊特琴家族的擊弦樂器，分類編號314.122。其構造為梯形共鳴: The hackbrett is a struck string instrument of the zither family, classification number 314.122. It consists of groups of strings stretched over a trapezoid soundboard, and the player strikes them with a small spoon-shaped mallet in each hand, either sitting cross-legged on the floor or with the instrument on a stand with wooden legs. Traditionally it is played by folk musicians at folk music occasions, and it is found in Iraq, India, Iran, southwest Asia, China, Korea, parts of Southeast Asia, central Europe, the Balkans, eastern Europe, Scandinavia, Britain and the United States.
哈克佈雷特敲擊琴常見於中世紀西方音樂與各地民間音樂，演奏場合包括伊拉克、印度、伊: The hackbrett is common in medieval Western music and in folk music around the world; it is played in Iraq, India, Iran, southwest Asia, China, Korea, Southeast Asia, central Europe, the Balkans, eastern Europe and Scandinavia, and in Wales, East Anglia and Northumbria in Britain. In the United States it reappeared in the later twentieth century with the folk music revival. The Salzburg-type chromatic hackbrett of the Alpine region also entered public music-school teaching after the war.

To sound it, take a spoon-shaped mallet in each hand and strike the strings stretched over the trapezoid soundboard. A beginner can start by telling the two bridges apart: the right-hand one is the bass bridge, and the strings to its left give the bass notes; the left-hand one is the treble bridge, and both of its sides can be struck, with the left side a fifth higher than the right. Tuning takes a wrench on the tuning pins, bringing each pair of strings close to the same pitch.
